title: Mathurā
summary: The holy city where Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared in the prison of Kaṁsa.
body:
Mathurā is one of the oldest holy cities of India, on the bank of the Yamunā. In the Bhāgavatam it is the capital of the Yadu dynasty, ruled in that period by the tyrant Kaṁsa.

It was in Kaṁsa's prison here that Kṛṣṇa appeared to Devakī and Vasudeva. Years later Kṛṣṇa returned from Vraja to Mathurā and ended Kaṁsa's rule.

Listed in Sivarama Maharaja's Pastime Places catalogue as: Great Forests (Adhivanas). Source: https://vanachari.blogspot.com/2023/12/pastime-places.html

title: Vṛndāvana
summary: The forest of Vraja on the Yamunā where Kṛṣṇa spent his childhood with the cowherd boys and the cows.
body:
Vṛndāvana is part of the pastoral land of Vraja. It is described as a place of beautiful forests, the Yamunā, hills and meadows, full of birds, peacocks and cows.

The Bhāgavatam describes the residents of Vraja moving there, and here Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma grazed the cows with their friends and performed many of the pastimes that are remembered by devotees to this day.

title: Govardhana Hill
summary: The sacred hill in Vraja that Kṛṣṇa lifted to protect the residents from Indra's storm.
body:
Govardhana is a hill in Vraja that provided grass and water for the cows of the cowherd community. It is regarded by devotees as non-different from the Lord.

Its best-known story is the one in which Kṛṣṇa held it up like an umbrella to shelter the people of Vraja from a devastating rain.

title: Madhuvana
summary: The forest on the Yamunā where young Dhruva practised austerity and saw the Lord.
body:
Madhuvana is a forest on the bank of the Yamunā. Nārada instructed Dhruva to go there to practise his worship.

Dhruva stayed there, steadily increasing his austerity, until the Lord appeared before him.

title: Kurukṣetra
summary: The field where the Bhagavad-gītā was spoken between two armies.
body:
Kurukṣetra is an ancient field of sacrifice and pilgrimage. It is best known as the site of the great war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas.

Just before the fighting began, Kṛṣṇa, acting as Arjuna's charioteer, spoke the Bhagavad-gītā here.

title: Sri Madana-mohana Temple
summary: Vṛndāvana temple of Śrī Rādhā-Madan Mohan, associated with Sanātana Gosvāmī and the Gauḍīya line from Śrī Caitanya.
body:
Deity: Śrī Rādhā-Madan Mohan. Sanātana Gosvāmī is named as the main Gosvāmī connected with this temple.

Dīkṣā-guru: Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu; direct initiation is traditionally accepted in Gauḍīya accounts. Śikṣā-guru: also Śrī Caitanya.

Lineage: Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Sanātana Gosvāmī. Sanātana was personally instructed for two months in Vārāṇasī by Mahāprabhu.

Region: Vṛndāvana. Listed in the Kartika-vrata itinerary for 25 Oct.

Vajranābha tradition: Śrī Madana-Mohana was originally installed in Vṛndāvana and was later taken to Karauli.

title: Sri Radha-Damodara Temple
summary: Vṛndāvana temple of Śrī Rādhā-Dāmodara, associated with Jīva Gosvāmī and the writing of Caitanya-caritāmṛta.
body:
Deity: Śrī Rādhā-Dāmodara. Jīva Gosvāmī is named as the main Gosvāmī connected with this temple. Rūpa Gosvāmī, his uncle, was his dīkṣā-guru. Jīva is considered the principal systematizer of Gauḍīya theology.

Lineage: Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Rūpa Gosvāmī → Jīva Gosvāmī.

Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja Gosvāmī lived and wrote at Rādhā-Dāmodara. He is famous as the author of Caitanya-caritāmṛta, which he wrote in advanced age, systematizing the theology of Rūpa and Raghunātha.

Kṛṣṇadāsa's dīkṣā-guru and śikṣā-guru were Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī. He also drew inspiration from Svarūpa Dāmodara through preserved notes. His lineage is given as Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Raghunātha dāsa Gosvāmī → Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja.

Region: Vṛndāvana. Listed in the Kartika-vrata itinerary for 27 Oct.

title: Sri Radha-Gokulananda Temple
summary: Vṛndāvana temple of Rādhā-Gokulānanda, connected with Lokanātha Gosvāmī, Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī and Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura.
body:
Deities: several, including Vijaya Govinda and Rādhā-Vinoda. Lokanātha Gosvāmī is the Gosvāmī connected with this temple.

Dīkṣā-guru: Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, traditionally accepted. Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura is named as Lokanātha's famous disciple.

Lineage: Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Lokanātha Gosvāmī.

Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī was a close associate of Lokanātha. He assisted in discovering holy places in Vṛndāvana, lived in deep renunciation, and helped establish early Vraja bhajana sites. His dīkṣā-guru is traditionally accepted as Śrī Caitanya, with the lineage Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī.

Region: Vṛndāvana. Listed in the Kartika-vrata itinerary for 29 Oct.

title: Datihā
summary: Ancient village where Kṛṣṇa's fight with Dantavakra is remembered.
body:
Datihā is an old village on the route from Satohā toward Nandagrāma. Tradition connects it with Dantavakra, whom Kṛṣṇa defeated here before leaving His weapons and crossing the Yamunā to meet the Vraja-vāsīs.

The adjoining Mayūra grove is recalled as a place of quiet meetings between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, served by the gopīs and watched by the forest peacocks.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Gandheśvara
summary: Perfume garden where Kṛṣṇa tested scents while thinking of Rādhā.
body:
Gandheśvara is remembered as a garden of fragrance near Koṭikā, with Gandharva-kuṇḍa at its centre. Vraja's perfume-makers once kept flower gardens here and distilled scents from seasonal blossoms, woods and musk.

Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd boys came here while grazing. The text recalls Kṛṣṇa asking Subala which fragrance would best attract Rādhā, and even taking the form of a perfume seller to reach Her.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Chaṭīkarā
summary: Early home of Nanda's family and a setting for Kṛṣṇa's childhood cowherd life.
body:
Chaṭīkarā is remembered as a place where Nanda Mahārāja's family lived before his move to Nandīśvara, which later became Nandagrāma. It therefore belongs to the earlier chapter of Kṛṣṇa's life among the cowherds.

From here the boys once drove their calves to the lake at Khadiravana, where Bakāsura attacked them. The site recalls both the household life of Nanda and the dangers that surrounded Kṛṣṇa's boyhood pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Dakṣiṇa (Jakhīna)
summary: Village also called Jakhīna, remembered for Rādhā's unusual surrender and Balarāma's victory over a yakṣiṇī.
body:
Dakṣiṇa, also known as Jakhīna, lies between Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā and Toṣa. Devotees remember that Rādhā, who is usually playful and contrary in Her love, became completely gentle and yielding to Kṛṣṇa here.

The name Jakhīna is linked to a female spirit who troubled the area until Balarāma subdued her. Several pools nearby honour Balarāma, Revatī, Jamadagni and Reṇukā.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Nima-grāma
summary: Village near Govardhana where the elder gopīs welcomed Kṛṣṇa after the lifting of the hill.
body:
Nima-grāma, set in a small grove of nima trees facing Sauṅkarāi, is linked with the pastime after Kṛṣṇa replaced Govardhana Hill. The elderly women of Vraja came here to embrace Him, wipe the perspiration from His brow and offer Him ārati with tears of affection.

The text also connects the place with Nimbārka Svāmī, who later lived in Nimavana and worshipped Kṛṣṇa there according to the Kumāra-sampradāya.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Gāṅṭhuli
summary: Village where the Deity Gopāla granted special audience to Caitanya Mahāprabhu.
body:
Gāṅṭhuli-grāma is remembered for the pastime in which Gopāla left Govardhana so that Caitanya Mahāprabhu could see Him for three days. A similar arrangement later allowed Rūpa Gosvāmī and his associates to have Gopāla's darśana in Mathurā.

The site therefore recalls both Caitanya's visit to Govardhana and the Gosvāmīs' deep longing for the Deity's company.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Beheja
summary: Village listed on the Govardhana and outer Vraja parikrama routes.
body:
Beheja appears in the Bhauma Vraja parikrama list between Gāṅṭhuli and Ḍīg, and again on the outer circuit near Samāi. The NVM gives no separate pastime for it.

It is kept as a named holy stop in the sacred geography of Vraja, where pilgrims walk in memory of Kṛṣṇa's life among the cowherds.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Sehu
summary: A halt on the Govardhana-side parikrama near Kedāranātha and Indrolī.
body:
Sehu is named in the traditional list of pastime places between Kedāranātha and Indrolī. The NVM does not tell a separate story about it.

Devotees honour it as part of the circuit around Govardhana, where each village and grove recalls some aspect of Kṛṣṇa's cowherd pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Satavāsa
summary: Eastern place where Rādhā and Satrājit are remembered for worship of the sun.
body:
Satavāsa is described as a place that first receives the rising sun on the eastern side of the dhāma. The text remembers Rādhā's devotion here and a lake called Sūrya-kuṇḍa, beside which Satrājit once worshipped the sun god.

The associated Syamantaka story is a warning that even powerful worship can be spoiled by impure motives, while simple devotion to the divine couple is the true goal.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Vanacārī (Vanacāriyā)
summary: Garden where the cowherd boys discussed whether Kṛṣṇa was a gopa or a forest dweller.
body:
Vanacārī, also called Vanacāriyā, is a garden where the gopas rested their cows while Kṛṣṇa was away. In His absence they debated whether their friend was truly a cowherd like them or a forest dweller who merely tended cattle.

The place thus preserves the intimate, questioning affection of the boys, who could not quite contain Kṛṣṇa within an ordinary social category.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Gendokhara (Gendo)
summary: Level field where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma played ball with the cowherd boys.
body:
Gendokhara is a level playing field near Nandagrāma where Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and their friends played with a ball. The boys came here after the morning milking or on the way to the pastures.

The text recalls Rādhā watching Kṛṣṇa's play from a nearby bush and wishing that She too could sport with Him with the same freedom as the gopas.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Chaṭa
summary: A small halt on the Nanda-grāma section of the Vraja parikrama.
body:
Chaṭa is named in the itinerary after Khadiravana and before Yāvaṭā and Kokilavana. The NVM gives no separate pastime for the place.

It is retained as part of the sacred route through which pilgrims remember the cowherd life of Nanda's village and the forests where Kṛṣṇa grazed the calves.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Kāmara
summary: Forest-village area linked with water brought forth for thirsty cowherd boys.
body:
Kāmara is associated in the text with Kāmaravana, where Kṛṣṇa's flute play is remembered as bringing forth water for His friends. The boys had become so absorbed in youth and play that they forgot food and drink until one of them suddenly cried out that he was thirsty.

The place recalls Kṛṣṇa's care for even the smallest needs of those who stay close to Him.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Rāsolī
summary: Secluded grove where Kṛṣṇa danced the rāsa with the gopīs beneath a banyan tree.
body:
Rāsolī takes its name from the rāsa dance Kṛṣṇa performed here on the bank of Rāsa-kuṇḍa. A great banyan tree with spreading roots gave shelter to the dancers and added a playful zigzag pattern to their movements.

The text remembers this as a quiet place near Kośīkalā, where Kṛṣṇa called the gopīs with His flute when they were visiting their parents around Varṣāṇā.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Dahgaon
summary: Village named on the woodland route between Rāsolī and Koṭaravana.
body:
Dahgaon is listed among the pastime places after Rāsolī and before Koṭaravana. No individual pastime is narrated for it in the NVM.

It is included as a named stop on the traditional circuit, honoured as part of the forest landscape in which Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs enacted their confidential pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Koṭaravana
summary: Secluded forest on Varṣāṇā's western side with lakes recalling sun worship and rāsa pastimes.
body:
Koṭaravana is described as a dense, conch-shaped forest covering Varṣāṇā's western side, near Dāna-, Māna- and Mora-gaṛh. The text mentions a Sūrya-kuṇḍa here where Rādhā and Her friends worshipped the sun god.

Nearby lakes such as Rāsa-kuṇḍa and Muktā-kuṇḍa keep the memory of Kṛṣṇa's dancing and of Rādhā's love, so the forest belongs to the quieter, interior circuit of Vraja.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Kośīkalā (Kośī)
summary: Sacred town also called Kuśasthalī, visited by the gopīs on pilgrimage.
body:
Kośīkalā, also named Kuśasthalī in the text, is a holy town whose Gomatī-kuṇḍa was sought by the gopīs for bathing. Their outing becomes a pastime in which Kṛṣṇa accompanies them through forest paths and lengthens the journey by His love.

The place joins the sanctity of Vraja's waters with the memory of the gopīs' pilgrimage and their affectionate exasperation with Kṛṣṇa's detours.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Ūjānī
summary: Yamunā-side stop remembered for the flute that turned the river's course.
body:
Ūjānī stands at the beginning of the riverbank section that continues to Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa. The text prays that the song of Kṛṣṇa's flute, which changed the course of the Yamunā here, may also turn wandering souls toward His feet.

The site belongs to the chain of Vraja pastimes in which the river, the cows, the cowherds and Kṛṣṇa's flute are all drawn together.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Vāndī
summary: Village on the pasture-land circuit between Lohavana and Baladeva/Daujī.
body:
Vāndī appears in the Bhauma Vraja list after Lohavana and before Baladeva, and also on the outer parikrama near Kayalo and Dhana-grāma. The NVM supplies no separate story for it.

It is preserved as a waypoint in the sacred geography where the childhood friendships of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma and the daily life of the cowherds are remembered.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Barifā
summary: Boundary place associated with the gopas' eating pastimes.
body:
Barifā lies at the edge of a petal of the dhāma and is counted among the boundary places of the parikrama. The text remembers it for the gopas' hearty eating during the winter season, when their youthful appetite was strongest.

The site keeps the lighter, household mood of Vraja līlā: food brought from home, fruit from the forest and the endless energy of the cowherd boys.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Kotharā
summary: Place where a Kuṇḍa refreshed Kṛṣṇa's cows near the edge of Vatsavana.
body:
Kotharā lies a short distance beyond Soṅkh, where the parikrama path turns toward Kāmyavana along a line of trees. Kotharā-kuṇḍa is remembered as fresh drinking water for Kṛṣṇa's cows before they returned home from this far corner of the dhāma.

A temple of Lord Nārāyaṇa now stands there, marking the place as part of the cowherds' practical and sacred landscape.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Devaśīrṣa
summary: Place where the demigods offered exalted prayers to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
body:
At Devaśīrṣa the demigods are remembered as offering their highest prayers to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Flowers showered by the devas and their wives are said to have formed the nearby kuṇḍa.

The text contrasts the demigods, who remained aware of their high positions, with sages who gave up false designations and attained the Lord through the dust of Vṛndāvana.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Pramodana (Pramodavana)
summary: Forest-village where Kṛṣṇa's presence brought delight to searching gopīs.
body:
Pramodana is linked with Pramodavana and the joy Kṛṣṇa gave the gopīs when they came looking for Him. In one remembered episode, their tears at not finding Him formed a stream that led them to where He was walking with Balarāma and the cows.

The name therefore holds both the sadness of separation and the delight of coming into the Lord's presence again.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Āṭora
summary: Secluded forest where Kṛṣṇa and the gopas lost track of a whole day in play.
body:
Āṭora is a secluded forest between the roads to Kāmyavana and Varṣāṇā. The text tells how Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, the cowherd boys and even the cows became so absorbed in play that twenty-four hours passed without anyone noticing.

Nanda Mahārāja searched through the night and found the boys only the next morning. The place celebrates the absorbing power of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes, which made a long night feel like a single moment.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Hara-Nārāyaṇa
summary: Place where Kṛṣṇa appeared in His four-armed Nārāyaṇa form during a cowherd prank.
body:
Hara-Nārāyaṇa is remembered for Kṛṣṇa's surprising appearance as the four-armed Lord while He was playing with the cowherd boys. His flute, turban and cowherd dress were hidden nearby, and the boys were freed from fear when He returned to His familiar form.

The gopīs also tested Him here, wanting to see whether the stories of His two extra arms were true. The place holds the playful meeting of Vraja intimacy and the Lord's fuller opulence.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Umrao
summary: Sacred spot where Rādhā was crowned queen of Vṛndāvana and Rādhā-vinoda was revealed.
body:
Umrao lies just south of Rahela, sheltered by a weeping willow. It is remembered as the place where Śrī Rādhā was crowned queen of Vṛndāvana; Kiśorī-kuṇḍa nearby recalls the bathing ceremony that accompanied Her coronation.

The text also tells how Kṛṣṇa appeared here with a Deity of Himself and gave it to Lokanātha Gosvāmī, who came to be known as Rādhā-vinoda.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Yamunā-mātā
summary: Yamunā-side stop where the river is honoured as a mother.
body:
Yamunā-mātā is a named stop on the riverbank section of the Vraja circuit. The text follows the same branch of the Yamunā past Parāsaulī, where Kṛṣṇa arranged a moonlit rāsa dance for the gopīs.

The place therefore joins the sanctity of the river herself with the memory of Kṛṣṇa's dancing and loving exchanges along her banks.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Pāpaḍī (Pāpaḍīvana)
summary: Flowering grove where the gopīs decorated Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa with petals.
body:
Pāpaḍī is the central grove of Pāpaḍīvana, named for the petal ornaments made here by the gopīs. They prepared garlands, crowns, a throne and festoons from soft flower petals to honour Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.

The place is remembered as an example of Vraja's natural opulence and of the gopīs' love expressed through simple forest flowers.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Didāvalī
summary: Village listed on both the Govardhana-side and outer Vraja parikrama routes.
body:
Didāvalī appears in the itinerary between Kotharā and Ādi-badri, and again on the outer circuit near Beheja and Khoṅha. The NVM gives it no independent pastime narrative.

It is included as one of the named villages of the sacred circuit, where pilgrims remember Kṛṣṇa's presence in the everyday life of Vraja.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Paśupā
summary: Grove where cows followed Kṛṣṇa's and Balarāma's scent and found Their hiding place.
body:
Paśupā is a grove in Paśupāvana where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma once hid from Their friends while playing. The cows tracked the brothers by Their bodily fragrance, and the boys followed the cows' hoofprints.

The name is remembered as a meeting of paśu, the cow, and pā, the track: the animals themselves become the guides that lead the cowherds back to Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Phalain
summary: Area of Prahlāda-kuṇḍa associated with Holī and Prahlāda's deliverance.
body:
Phalain is known for Prahlāda-kuṇḍa and the annual Holikā-dahan and colour festival held nearby. The story remembered here is Prahlāda's unwavering faith in Lord Viṣṇu, which protected him from Hiraṇyakaśipu's cruel attempts.

The text adds that Kṛṣṇa recalled Prahlāda's example each spring, making the festival a living reminder that the Lord protects His devotee.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Kerala
summary: Grazing field where Kṛṣṇa rested beneath a tree and dreamed of meeting Rādhā.
body:
Kerala is a field in Vraja where Kṛṣṇa is remembered as grazing the cows after Loṭana-kuṇḍa. At its southern edge stands a tree whose exposed root He once used as a seat.

Leaning against the trunk with His eyes closed, He dreamed of the meeting with Rādhā that would take place later that night. The place joins the ordinary work of herding with the inner world of Kṛṣṇa's love.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Gopī-ghāṭa
summary: Yamunā bathing place of the gopīs before Kṛṣṇa took their clothes.
body:
Gopī-ghāṭa is one of the three sites connected with the Kātyāyanī-vrata pastime: Tapovana, where the gopīs performed austerity, this ghāṭa, where they bathed in the Yamunā, and Cīra-ghāṭa, where Kṛṣṇa took their garments.

The place recalls the young women of Vṛndāvana asking goddess Kātyāyanī for Kṛṣṇa as their husband and then meeting Him in the riverbank pastime that followed.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Kayalo
summary: Village named just after Viśrāma-ghāṭa on the outer Vraja circuit.
body:
Kayalo appears in the Bhauma Vraja list immediately after Viśrāma-ghāṭa. The NVM does not narrate a separate pastime for it.

It is retained as a named stop on the outer parikrama, belonging to the route on which pilgrims remember Kṛṣṇa's departures from Vraja and His return to the cowherds.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Dhana-grāma
summary: Village at the edge of Nanda's domain where Balarāma is worshipped.
body:
Dhana-grāma stands at the extreme tip of Tālavana, where the text places the boundary of Nanda Mahārāja's domain. Lord Balarāma is still worshipped here.

The site recalls the borderland of the cowherd kingdom and the affectionate regard in which the Vraja-vāsīs hold Kṛṣṇa's elder brother.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Soṅkh
summary: Boundary place where the aroma of the gopīs' cooking attracted Kṛṣṇa.
body:
Soṅkh is one of the boundary places on the parikrama, remembered for the scent of the gopīs' cooking that reached Kṛṣṇa here. Local tradition also speaks of Soṅkh-kuṇḍa, where that fragrance is said still to linger.

The site belongs to the Vraja pastimes of food and hospitality, in which Kṛṣṇa is drawn by the loving service of the cowherd women.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Vatsa-grāma
summary: Village associated with Vatsavana and the early grazing pastimes of Vraja.
body:
Vatsa-grāma is listed on the outer parikrama near Soṅkh and Samāi. It is naturally linked with Vatsavana, the forest where Kṛṣṇa first led the calves out to graze.

The place recalls the simple village life of Nanda's household and the boyhood pastimes of the calves, the cows and the young cowherds.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Samāi
summary: Garden where Kṛṣṇa disguised Himself as a gopī to approach Rādhā.
body:
Samāi is a garden near Śyāma-ḍhāk whose name is connected with Śyāmā-sakhī. When Rādhā was displeased after a rāsa festival and would not be pacified, Kṛṣṇa followed Viśākhā's advice and came to Her dressed as that gopī.

The disguise allowed Him to turn Rādhā's indifference into longing. The place therefore belongs to the delicate pastimes of reconciliation in Vraja.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Khoṅha
summary: Playing field where Rādhā and Her friends played kho-kho.
body:
Khoṅha is remembered as an open field where Rādhā and the gopīs played kho-kho, a chasing game related to tag. The text describes the divine couple watching one another with curiosity and delight while absorbed in such childish play.

The area is also associated with the sacred field where the samādhis of Caitanya Mahāprabhu's principal associates are honoured.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Bādalī
summary: Orchard where Kṛṣṇa brought a cooling cloud to relieve the heat.
body:
Bādalī is a forest orchard where Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd boys once sheltered from fierce midday heat. The boys fanned Him with blossoming branches and asked whether He could do something about the sun.

A cloud then spread above them like an umbrella and showered fine drops, turning the place into a cool spring-like grove. The pastime shows Kṛṣṇa's responsiveness to even the small complaints of His friends.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Pāi-grāma
summary: Village on the outer parikrama between Bhojana-thālī and Śṛṅgāra.
body:
Pāi-grāma is named in the Bhauma Vraja itinerary after Bhojana-thālī and before Pinthānā and Śṛṅgāra. The NVM gives no separate narrative for it.

It is kept as a waypoint in the sacred circuit where pilgrims remember Kṛṣṇa's daily rounds with the cows and the Uddhava-associated places of the outer path.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Pinthānā
summary: Village named on the outer Vraja parikrama near Pāi-grāma and Sondha.
body:
Pinthānā appears between Pāi-grāma and Śṛṅgāra in the traditional list. No distinct pastime is told about it in the NVM.

The entry preserves the name as part of the sacred map of Vraja, honoured as one of the places remembered by those who walk the outer circuit.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Sondha
summary: Home of Sannanda, Nanda Mahārāja's wise brother and counsellor.
body:
Sondha is remembered as the residence of Sannanda, also called Sunanda, Nanda Mahārāja's younger brother. He is described as a trusted counsellor who advised Nanda to move from Gokula to Vṛndāvana and to accept Kṛṣṇa's proposal to worship Govardhana instead of Indra.

The site recalls the wise elder statesman of Vraja and his role in shaping the cowherd community's response to Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Khambī (Khambi)
summary: Place with a sacred pillar reminding pilgrims not to abandon Vṛndāvana.
body:
Khambī is remembered for a pillar that warns conditioned souls never to turn away from Kṛṣṇa and leave the shelter of Vṛndāvana. The text connects it with the southern petal of the dhāma and the transition into Hāsyavana.

The place thus carries a practical spiritual lesson as well as a memory of Vraja's sacred landscape.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Hāsanapura
summary: Capital of Vraja's humorous mellow in the forest of Hāsyavana.
body:
Hāsanapura is the sacred settlement associated with Hāsyavana, the forest of humour. The text remembers the gopas sitting in a circle at lunch while Kṛṣṇa appeared to be seated beside each of them at once.

Echoes of their laughter are said to be heard by liberated souls in the trees, and the place preserves the joyful, playful side of Kṛṣṇa's Vraja pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Mārava-grāma (Mārava)
summary: Yamunā-bank āśrama of Mārkaṇḍeya Ṛṣi.
body:
Mārava-grāma, also called Mārava, is identified as Mārkaṇḍeya Ṛṣi's āśrama on the bank of the Yamunā. The sage is remembered for extraordinarily long and patient worship, sustained through many ages.

After a vision of Cosmic dissolution and the Lord's protection, he came to understand Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme and settled here to practise bhajana under the shelter of Vṛndāvana.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Jedapura
summary: Village on the southern stretch of the outer Vraja parikrama.
body:
Jedapura is listed between Hāsanapura and Bājanā on the outer circuit. The NVM does not give it a separate pastime.

It is included as part of the named sacred geography of Vraja, where even the smaller villages are honoured as places connected with Kṛṣṇa's presence.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Bājanā
summary: Village named between Jedapura and Salākā on the Vraja circuit.
body:
Bājanā appears in the traditional parikrama list after Jedapura. The document provides no individual story for the place.

It is retained as a named stop in the sacred landscape, remembered by pilgrims as they pass through the southern villages of Vraja.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Salākā
summary: Named halt on the outer Vraja parikrama near Bājanā and Pitorā.
body:
Salākā is listed between Bājanā and Pitorā. No separate pastime is narrated in the NVM.

The entry preserves it as one of the places in the traditional itinerary through which the whole land of Vraja is regarded as a field of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Pitorā
summary: Village in the southern group of outer Vraja parikrama stops.
body:
Pitorā is named after Salākā and before Ṭetī-grāma in the Bhauma Vraja list. The NVM gives no distinct episode associated with it.

It is included as a waypoint in the sacred circuit, part of the network of villages that preserve the memory of Kṛṣṇa's life in Vraja.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Ṭetī-grāma
summary: Village named between Pitorā and Jāravā on the outer circuit.
body:
Ṭetī-grāma appears in the outer Vraja parikrama list without a detailed pastime in the NVM.

It is kept as a named sacred place in the itinerary, where pilgrims remember Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma moving among the cowherd settlements of Vraja.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Jāravā
summary: Village listed near Ṭetī-grāma and Rāya on the outer Vraja route.
body:
Jāravā is named in the traditional list between Ṭetī-grāma and Rāya. The document supplies no standalone pastime for it.

The place is preserved as part of the sacred circuit of Vraja, honoured as one of the many settlements within the land of Kṛṣṇa's manifest pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Rāya
summary: Small place named between Jāravā and Kārabha in the outer Vraja list.
body:
Rāya appears in the Bhauma Vraja itinerary between Jāravā and Kārabha. No individual story is told about it in the NVM passage.

It is included as a named stop on the sacred parikrama route, part of the wider landscape in which devotees remember Kṛṣṇa's cowherd pastimes.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Kārabha
summary: Village named near Rāya and Vāndī in the outer Vraja circuit.
body:
Kārabha is listed after Rāya and before Vāndī in the traditional itinerary. The NVM gives it no separate pastime account.

It is retained as part of the sacred geography of Vraja, where the villages themselves become reminders of the Lord's presence among the cowherds.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Bali-ṭīlā
summary: Raised mound where Bali Mahārāja performed the Viśvajit sacrifice.
body:
Bali-ṭīlā is a raised mound inland from Sūrya-ghāṭa where Bali Mahārāja is remembered as performing the Viśvajit sacrifice. The place is associated with his seeking power and his eventual surrender to Lord Vāmana.

Devotees pray here for the gift of unconditional surrender, taking Bali as an example of a king whose pride was transformed by the Lord.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Sītā-Rāma
summary: Garden where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa played the roles of Sītā and Rāma.
body:
Sītā-Rāma is a garden where the divine couple are remembered as taking the forms of Sītā and Lord Rāmacandra in exile. The cowherd boys often acted out the Rāmāyaṇa, and the gopīs asked Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa to reveal Themselves as the royal pair.

A cottage here commemorates the place where They adorned Themselves as forest exiles, allowing devotees to enter that pastime through meditation.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Nīgānyā
summary: Place where the gopīs cross-examined Kṛṣṇa during a pilgrimage to Kośīkalā.
body:
Nīgānyā is where the gopīs finally stopped Kṛṣṇa after He had led them on a long, scenic detour when they were travelling to Kośīkalā. They had set out to bathe in Gomatī-kuṇḍa but found themselves in the middle of the forest.

Rādhā challenged Him about the supposed shortcut, and the place preserves the playful cross-examination that revealed how much He wanted to lengthen the time with His beloved friends.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Agravana
summary: Forest where Caitanya Mahāprabhu first entered Vraja in ecstasy.
body:
Agravana is a remote forest where Caitanya Mahāprabhu is remembered as first entering Vraja from Prayāga. Overcome by love, He rolled on the ground, embraced the trees and called on the animals and plants to chant Kṛṣṇa's name.

The site also contains older tīrthas such as Reṇukā-āśrama and Paraśurāma's birthplace, joining the Mathurā-Vṛndāvana memories with Caitanya's own arrival in the dhāma.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Surabhivana
summary: Govardhana forest where Surabhi and Indra bathed Kṛṣṇa.
body:
Surabhivana is an expansive forest reaching toward Govinda-kuṇḍa. The text remembers Surabhi and Indra bathing Kṛṣṇa here; the water from that abhiṣeka formed the pool known as Govinda-kuṇḍa.

The pastime establishes Kṛṣṇa as the king and shelter of the cows, and the forest remains associated with that moment of honour and delight.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Premavana
summary: Love-saturated forest surrounding Prema-sarovara.
body:
Premavana is the forest at the heart of which lies Prema-sarovara. Its grasses, vines and trees are described as nourished by the lake's water, which represents a rare and confidential form of transcendental love.

The site includes a temple of Prema-bihārī, a platform recalling the rāsa dance and a swing where the divine couple are said to sport. It is the woodland counterpart of the existing Prema-sarovara entry.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Candra-kūpa
summary: Sacred well listed beside Candra-sarovara among Vraja's ten wells.
body:
Candra-kūpa is one of the ten sacred wells listed in the NVM appendix, associated here with Candra-sarovara. The text gives it no extended narrative.

It is recorded as part of Vraja's network of holy waters, remembered by pilgrims alongside the other kūpas that sustained and sanctified the cowherd settlements.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Bhāṇḍīra-kūpa
summary: Well near Bhāṇḍīravana, listed among Vraja's ten sacred wells.
body:
Bhāṇḍīra-kūpa is named among the ten wells of Vraja in the area of Bhāṇḍīravana. The surrounding grove is famous for Kṛṣṇa's wrestling with the cowherd boys and gopīs, His swallowing of the forest fire, and Balarāma's defeat of Pralamba.

The well belongs to that same Yamunā-side landscape of play, danger and divine protection.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)

title: Karaṇavedha-kūpa
summary: Sacred well at Gokula included among Vraja's ten wells.
body:
Karaṇavedha-kūpa is listed among the ten wells of Vraja and is placed at Gokula, the early home of Nanda Mahārāja. The appendix gives no detailed story for this particular well.

It is preserved as part of the holy water system of Vraja, remembered alongside Nanda-kūpa, Indra-kūpa, Kṛṣṇa-kūpa and the other wells connected with the cowherd settlements.
source_ref: Śivarāma Swami, Nava-vraja-mahimā, vols. 1–8 (user-provided; original summary)
